sn55.1:1.3: The legendary wheel-turning monarch, who ruled without violence from sea to sea, is depicted in detail in [dn17]() and [dn26]().
sn55.1:2.1: These are the four factors of stream-entry. The devotional passages that follow are regularly recited throughout Theravadin communities, and also form the basis of meditation on the triple gem.
sn55.1:2.2: “Experiential” is _avecca_, literally “having undergone”. “Experiential confidence” is the faith of a stream-enterer, who has seen for themselves.
sn55.1:2.3: _Bhagavā_ (“blessed one”, “lord”) is the normal honorific for the Buddha in Pali; normally I translate it as “the Buddha”. The literal meaning is “one who has good fortune”, in which sense it stems from Vedic times (Rig Veda 7.41.5). In Pali it is used only for the Buddha, but elsewhere was a general honorific used, for example, by King Janaka to address Yajñavalkya (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.14), among respected peers (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.8.7), to a teacher (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.4.3), or by Manu to his daughter (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.8.1.9). | _Buddha_ (“awakened one”) is used in Pali especially of Siddhattha Gotama himself, but occasionally as a general term for those who are enlightened. The idea of “awakening” is found throughout the Vedic texts, often associated with the Dawn (RV 1.113.4). | _Arahant_ (“perfected one”, literally “worthy”) is used for the Buddha and others who have realized full awakening. Originally an epithet of the “worthy gods” deserving of praise and sacrifice (eg. RV 1.94.1, 1.127.06, 1.134.6, 5.7.2, 5.52.5, 5.86.5; ŚB 3.4.1.3). | _Vijjācaraṇasampanna_ (“accomplished in knowledge and conduct”) is explained in detail at [dn3](). | For _sugata_ (“holy”) see note on [sn38.3:1.4](). | _Lokavidū_ may be explained as singular—knowing the cosmos inside a person ([sn2.26]())—or plural—knowing the worlds, sometimes numbered three ([tha-ap535:26.2](); cf. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16). | The Buddha’s training is often compared to taming a fine horse or elephant (eg. [mn65:33.1](), [mn107:3.2]()). | The Buddha’s role as teacher of gods is emphasized in SN 1, SN 2, SN 6, and many places throughout the canon.
sn55.1:2.5: _Sandiṭṭhika_ and _akālika_ (“apparent in the present life, immediately effective”) are synonyms, as are _anantara_ and _diṭṭheva dhamme_, all of which mean “in the present life, without delay or interim”, in contrast with _samparāyika_ (“pertaining to lives to come”; see eg. [mn13:8.5]()). | _Ehipassika_ (“inviting inspection”) is literally “come-and-see-ish”. | For “relevant”, see note on [sn55.7:3.1](). | “Sensible people” is _viññū_, “knowing ones”. | All these epithets seem primarily Buddhist.
sn55.1:2.7: The suttas distinguish between two senses of Saṅgha. The “mendicant Saṅgha” (_bhikkhusaṅgha_) is the conventional community of monks and nuns. The “Saṅgha of disciples” (_sāvakasaṅgha_) is classified as fourfold according to the stages of awakening: stream-entry, once-return, non-return, and perfection. Each of these stages is further subdivided into those of the path who are practicing for realization and those of the fruit who have realized. These are referred to as “noble disciples”, four of the path and four of the fruit, making eight individuals in total. Saṅgha is not used in the sense of “spiritual community”. | “Religious donation” is _dakkhiṇa_, the fee paid to Vedic priests for their services; for details see [mn142:5.1]().
